::: {.graybox}
In the manuscript entitled “Learning the Shape of Evolutionary Landscapes:
Geometric Deep Learning Reveals Hidden Structure in Phenotype-to-Fitness Maps,”
the authors apply an existing dimensionality reduction method (RHVAE) to
multi-dimensional data from experimental evolution. They propose interpreting
the latent space learned from the data as a representation of the organism’s
phenotypic space.

The authors first attempt to validate this idea using artificial data, where
evolutionary dynamics are simulated under simplifying assumptions. The generated
data is processed using three dimensionality reduction methods, PCA, a “vanilla”
VAE, and RHVAE, and the authors compare their performance based on geometric
similarity between the ground-truth phenotypic space and the learned latent
space. They conclude that RHVAE better captures the underlying structure of the
phenotype space. These methods are then applied to a set of real data obtained
by another group (Iwasawa et al., 2022), and the authors claim that the
VAE-based approaches can “predict” the fitness of a cell population in a new
condition.

Although the manuscript is relatively clear in explaining what was done, I do
not think it convincingly validates its central claim that RHVAE, when applied
to high-dimensional fitness data, can capture the structure of phenotypic space.
The resemblance between the latent space and the ground-truth phenotype space in
a specific simulation does not imply that RHVAE can reliably extract phenotypic
structure from real data, especially when the simulation setting appears
oversimplified (see below). In addition, the proposed analysis does not seem to
yield any new insights into the real evolutionary experiment. The authors’ claim
that their method can “predict” fitness in a new environment is undermined by
the fact that such a “prediction” requires actual data from that new
environment. It is therefore unclear how this constitutes a meaningful
prediction if the experiment must be performed beforehand.

For these reasons, I do not believe this manuscript meets the standards of PRX
Life. At this stage, it is unclear whether the work offers sufficient novelty or
insight to merit publication even in a more specialized journal. 
:::

## Major concerns

::: {.graybox}
1. The simulation setting appears to overlook the complexity of
evolutionary adaptation.

- In particular, it neglects a fundamental property of cells: their ability to
physiologically adapt to new environments through changes in gene expression.
Incorporating this property would likely require fundamental changes in how the
latent space extracted from fitness data is interpreted.
:::

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment, which allows us to clarify a
crucial aspect of our modeling framework. We agree that our model does not
explicitly simulate the dynamics of physiological adaptation, such as changes in
gene expression. However, our definition of "phenotype" is broad enough to
encompass these complex, time-varying characteristics within a fixed coordinate
in phenotypic space.

This approach builds upon the long tradition in evolutionary biology of using
simplified genotype-phenotype-fitness relationships, with the fitness landscape
being the canonical example [@orr2005]. In this tradition, even dynamic or
stochastic traits are represented by their underlying, genetically-determined
parameters.

For instance, consider the reviewer's example of physiological adaptation
through gene expression. A specific genotype defines the regulatory network that
governs the expression of certain genes in response to environmental cues. While
the expression levels themselves may fluctuate over time, the parameters
defining the *response function*---such as the induction threshold or the
maximum expression level---are stable characteristics of that genotype. These
parameters can be treated as the coordinates in our phenotypic space. A mutation
might alter a promoter region, leading to a new genotype with a different
induction threshold, and thus, a different, fixed coordinate in the phenotypic
space.

Therefore, while our framework simplifies the dynamic process, it is capable of
capturing the heritable variation in the *rules* that govern physiological
adaptation. The latent space we extract from fitness data can thus be
interpreted as representing these underlying parameters that define a cell's
adaptive capabilities.

To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the manuscript:

> Figure 1(A) shows a schematic of the genotype-phenotype-fitness map. A genotype
$g$ produces a set of measurable traits or phenotypes $\underline{p}$---depicted
as two potential molecular phenotypes, such as an efflux pump rate and the
sensitivity of a membrane receptor. 
<span style="color: #912E27;"> 
Following the tradition in evolutionary biology, we take the most general
definition of phenotype, which includes time-varying organism characteristics as
a single phenotype. In other words, any genetically-determined organism
characteristic---including time-varying features such as developmental time---is
considered a single phenotype.
</span>
The fitness of each genotype is determined
by the value of these phenotypes and the environment $E$---depicted as the
doubling time of a bacterial population. To formalize this mathematically, we
represent genotypes as points in a multi-dimensional phenotypic space, where
each dimension is a different trait ($\underline{p} \in \mathbb{R}^P$, where $P$
is the number of traits). Thus, any genotype $g$ has a unique mapping to a
phenotypic coordinate. 
<span style="color: #912E27;"> 
We emphasize again that even dynamically changing organism characteristics are
still defined by a single fixed coordinate in phenotype space [@fragata2019a].
</span>
However, this mapping is not necessarily bijective...

::: {.graybox}
- The dimensionality of phenotypic space is assumed to be very low (as low as
two dimensions), but it is unclear under what conditions this assumption is
validated. In the context of cellular adaptation to antibiotic environments,
relevant phenotypic traits may include membrane permeability, biofilm formation
(which involves quorum sensing, motility, etc.), metabolic state, cell
morphology, enzymatic degradation, and stress response, to name a few. Many of
these are dynamic and require multiple parameters to characterize. Thus, the
assumption that cellular phenotype can be captured by a few numbers seems rather
strong.

- Relatedly, the assumption that the dimensionality of phenotypic space is much
lower than that of the fitness data is quite strong. The dimensionality of the
data is set by the number of environments tested in an experiment. In most
cases, including Iwasawa et al., this number is small—their dataset has
dimensionality of only eight. Given the complexity of cellular phenotypes, it is
unclear whether this assumption holds in real-world settings. 
:::

We again thank the reviewer for this insightful comment, which allows us to
clarify a crucial aspect of our modeling framework.

Our work is inspired by the recent body of work suggesting that **effective**
phenotypic changes are low dimensional. Work coming from our own lab
[@kinsler2020], in which yeast populations adapted to minimal glucose media
found cells explore a low-dimensional phenotype space---as determined by a
linear rather than a nonlinear dimensionality reduction method. More recent work
from our lab [@ghosh2025] confirmed this finding, suggesting the existence of
"limiting functions"---organismal functions that, as the name suggests, limit
the organism's ability to adapt to new environments---creating "effective
phenotypes" or degrees of freedom that evolution can exploit to achieve adaption
to novel environments.

The experimental work in which we based our analysis [@iwasawa2022] found a
similar result utilizing a linear dimensionality reduction method in the context
of antibiotic resistance. The authors found that the phenotype space of a
bacterial population adapting to an antibiotic is low dimensional, even though
populations were exposed to different antibiotics, again suggesting the
existence of low-dimensional phenotype spaces in which adaptation takes place.

Furthermore, theoretical work from the group of Professor Kaneko
[@kaneko2015;@furusawa2018;@sato2020;@sato2023] points to the existence of these
low-dimensional phenotypic spaces. In this body of work, *in silico*-evolved
complex systems made of multiple interacting components converge to explore
effective low-dimensional degrees of freedom. More work in the literature,
summarized in the excellent review by @russo2025b, demonstrates that the
existence of these effective low-dimensional degrees of freedom are a widespread
phenomenon in biology. From the effectiveness of bacterial growth laws
[@Scott2010] in which the microscopic details of how this global observable can
be ignored, giving rise to effective degrees of freedom, to the existence of
community-function landscapes in microbial ecology [@skwara2023a] determining
community compositions from a few effective degrees of freedom.

Part of our argument is that harvesting the generality of deep neural networks
as function approximators can be used to extract these effective degrees of
freedom from high-dimensional data in an even more efficient way.

To emphasize this point, based on the reviewer's comment, we have added the
following text to the introduction:

> In this model, multiple
lineages perform a biased random walk on a low-dimensional phenotypic space
towards regions of higher fitness, defined by the environment-specific
topography of the fitness landscape. 
<span style="color: #912E27;"> 
Of course, the true phenotypic state of a
cell is controlled by many interacting variables---membrane permeability,
metabolic state, stress responses, and more. Our assumption is not that these
axes disappear, but that adaptation proceeds along effective, emergent
low-dimensional manifolds that summarize these complex processes [@kaneko2015;
@furusawa2018].
</span>
Changing the
environment, therefore, amounts to changing the landscape topography while
keeping the phenotypic coordinates of the lineages constant. We show that the
geometry-informed variational autoencoder (hereafter *RHVAE* for Riemannian
Hamiltonian Variational Autoencoder [@chadebec2020]) is able to learn a
low-dimensional embedding that retains information about the relative
positions of the simulated lineages in the original phenotypic space. 

Furthermore, in the discussion, we have added the following text:

> Our ability to experimentally track evolving microbial populations presents an
unprecedented opportunity to better understand the complexity of the space in
which evolutionary dynamics take place. The recent wave of work following the
strategy of determining the fitness of multiple genotypes, not in one, but
multiple environments [@kinsler2020; @iwasawa2022; @ascensao2023; @ghosh2025]
suggests that this is a powerful approach to try to uncover the underlying
structure of the genotype-phenotype-fitness map. Combined with the body of
theoretical work suggesting that the genotype-phenotype map is
low-dimensional---meaning that a large number of genotypes result in a small
number of distinct phenotypes [@kaneko2015; @louis2016; @furusawa2018;
@russo2025b]---there is hope that we can leverage these large-scale datasets to
uncover features of the phenotypic space underlying adaptation in a data-driven
way. 
<span style="color: #912E27;"> 
These studies support a view where, although cellular phenotype is
intrinsically high-dimensional, adaptation is constrained by a few effective
degrees of freedom. This distinction between mechanistic high dimensionality and
effective low dimensionality helps reconcile our assumption with the underlying
biological complexity.
</span>

::: {.graybox}
2. The condition under which their method is valid remains unclear

- The authors argue that the latent space learned from “high-dimensional fitness
profiles” can be interpreted as phenotypic space, based on a single simulation
setting that appears overly simplistic, as discussed above. However, even if the
simulation were sufficiently realistic, the resemblance between the latent space
and phenotypic space in one specific simulation does not imply that latent space
inferred from real data captures the structure of the phenotype space. Thus,
questions that need to be addressed include: How sensitive is the resemblance to
the experimental design, data quantity, or dimensionality? Is there any
theoretical justification for why one should expect the latent space to reflect
the structure of the phenotypic space? These questions are not addressed in the
manuscript, making it difficult to accept the proposed interpretation of the
latent space. 
:::

We thank the reviewer for mentioning these concerns with our work. We agree that
questions of sensitivity to the experimental design, data quantity, and
dimensionality are important to address. We have only briefly touched on these
points in the supplementary material, where we provide a comparison between the
predictions of a 2D vs. a 3D latent space on the @iwasawa2022 dataset. However,
a more thorough analysis of these points is beyond the scope of the present
manuscript, as it would require a more extensive dataset. We are more than happy
to expand on the limitations of our work in the manuscript.

As for the theoretical justification for why one should expect the latent space
to reflect the structure of the phenotypic space, we mentioned in the manuscript
the classic Fisher geometric model [@orr2005] as a general theoretical scaffold
widely used in evolutionary biology to describe the structure of phenotype
space. If anything, the model utilized in our simulations generalizes this
classic model, as it allows for the existence of more than one fitness peak
within the landscape. To the degree that the idea of a fitness landscape
captures any reality of the dynamics of evolution, the generality of neural
networks as function approximators should suffice to represent some aspects of
this structure in a data-driven way. We have softened the language
used in the manuscript to emphasize that the latent space is not necessarily a
scale-invariant map to the phenotype space but rather a map that captures some
aspects of the structure of this space. The degree to which this is a meaningful
map is a question that will depend on the specific application. More explicitly,
we have added the following text at the end of the section 2.1:

> <span style="color: #912E27;"> 
We stress that the latent space inferred by our framework should not be
interpreted as a one-to-one reconstruction of the full phenotypic space.
Rather, it captures effective structural features of the phenotype–fitness
relationship given the data available. The fidelity of this representation will
depend on experimental design, data quantity, and dimensionality, all of which
we only begin to explore here.
</span>

Furthermore, in the discussion, we have added the following text:

> <span style="color: #912E27;"> 
Our interpretation of latent space as a proxy for phenotypic space comes with
limitations. The degree to which this mapping is faithful depends on factors
such as data richness, experimental design, and the intrinsic dimensionality of
the underlying traits. A full sensitivity analysis will require larger and more
varied datasets, which is beyond the scope of the present work. Thus, our
results should be viewed as proof of principle rather than a definitive
characterization.
</span>

::: {.graybox}
3. It is unclear what new insights RHVAE provides when applied to real
data.

- The authors argue in section 2.7 that RHVAE “predicts” responses to a missing
antibiotic. However, this wording of “prediction” is misleading, since the data
from the “missing” antibiotic is required to make the prediction. The results
shown in this section seem to follow quite straightforwardly from those
presented in the previous section. Thus, the analysis conducted on real data
does not appear to yield any new insights into the data or enable predictions
about untested antibiotics. 
:::

We are grateful to the reviewer for highlighting this point. In our mind, this
comment is at the core of a philosophical debate of what prediction means in
science. Although, we agree that an ideal prediction would not require the use
of any data from the missing environment, giving a parameter-free prediction, we
are not aware of any method that can make such a prediction for such a complex
system without any parameter calibration.

Nevertheless, we consider our contribution to be meaningful in the sense that
the construction of the latent space did not contain any information about the
missing environment. However, because of the nature of deep learning methods,
only post-facto predictions can be made after calibrating the model on a subset
of the data. As we explain in the manuscript, this is analogous to what was done
by @kinsler2020 with linear models.

It is important to note that previous studies, including @kinsler2020 and
@iwasawa2022, relied on linear approximations for dimensionality reduction. At
the outset of our work, it was not obvious that a lower-dimensional nonlinear
mapping would perform as well as, or better than, these established full linear
approximations. Our findings demonstrate that nonlinear methods can indeed
capture the underlying structure more effectively, which represents a meaningful
advancement over the linear approaches used in prior work.

Our work does not address the full potential of the proposed methodology. The
power of the present computational framework can be further harnessed in the
limit of a larger number of environments and a larger number of mutants. We
imagine a scenario in which having a much more extensive dataset to calibrate
the model would allow for predictions of unseen phenotypes with a smaller number
of measurements for unseen mutants.

Moreover, the main goal of our work is to propose a conceptual framework with
which to address the need to understand the underlying structure of
high-dimensional fitness measurements that are increasingly being used in
evolutionary biology.

To address the reviewer's comment, we added the following text to the section 2.7:

> In essence, we use seven antibiotics to place each genotype in
latent space, then test how accurately these coordinates predict resistance to
the eighth antibiotic. 
<span style="color: #912E27;"> 
We emphasize that this prediction is not parameter-free:
the model must first be calibrated on the available environments. What is novel
is that the latent structure inferred without access to the missing antibiotic
nevertheless generalizes well, allowing us to reconstruct its response profile
post hoc. We direct interested readers to the Supplementary Material section E
for a detailed description of the of both approaches.
</span>

In the discussion, we have added the following text:

> <span style="color: #912E27;"> 
Our approach does not yet allow prediction of responses to completely unseen
antibiotics without calibration data. Rather, its contribution lies in
demonstrating that nonlinear latent variable models can capture the effective
structure of high-dimensional fitness profiles and generalize across held-out
environments. This shows that the low-dimensional manifold underlying adaptation
is robust enough to be recovered even when parts of the data are missing, a
point that was not guaranteed from prior linear approaches.
</span>
